sources.citation: Chantanakomes, Veena. 1980. A description of Moken: a Malayo-Polynesian language. MA thesis, Mahidol University. 359 pp. (Rawai/Phuket Moken; SEAlang Mahidol theses archive, http://www.sealang.net/archives/mahidol/Veena.pdf; image-only PDF, stress pages scanned)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: p.9: 'The Stress Group may have from one to two syllables ... Each Stress Group has only one major stressed syllable as nucleus and may have one unstressed syllable or one minor stressed syllable as periphery. Stress in Moken is predictable. In monosyllabic words, stress is on that syllable. In disyllabic words which are composed of Pre-Syllable + Major Syllable the first will [be] unstressed and the latter will take primary stress.' p.10: 'In disyllabic words which are composed of a minor + major syllable, the minor syllable will take the secondary and the major syllable primary stress.' p.12
sources.locator: thesis pp.9-12 (PDF pp.44-47), sect. 1.2 'The Stress Group (The Phonological Word)' and 1.2.4 'Word Boundaries'

sources.quote: 'words composed of a prefixed syllable and a major syllable will have stress placed on the major syllable. In other words, the last syllable will always be stressed and its absence gives clue to word breaks.' (verbatim as in record; unattributed in the article)

sources.citation: Pittayaporn, Pittayawat. 2005. Moken as a Mainland Southeast Asian language. In Anthony Grant & Paul Sidwell (eds.), Chamic and beyond: studies in mainland Austronesian languages, 189-210. Pacific Linguistics 569. Canberra: ANU. (sealang PL archive PL-569.189)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: p.191: 'Like other mainland languages, Moken has a strictly iambic word template. In other word[s], the canonical shape of Moken words is disyllabic, with a stressed second syllable: CVCV(:)(C). ... The major syllable takes the primary stress and always occupies the right edge of the word. It is the head of the word, its presence is obligatory.' p.199: 'a non-violable word-maximality constraint that requires that every Moken phonological word be an iambic foot.' p.189 quotes Larish 1999:381 that Moken 'may have adopted word-final stress under MK influence'.
sources.locator: p.191 (sect. 2 Phonology of Moken) and p.199
